title: Does a robust fit or a Kalman filter hold a camera's clock better between audio re-syncs than a least-squares line, once the clock drift comes from a real crystal curve?
summary: Follow-up to capture-syncslope on synthetic speech-like audio (capture-audiosync's GCC-PHAT, residual searched). Replaces its assumed 10–30 ppm rate wobble with a clock rate computed from the AT-cut crystal temperature curve in the Corning/Tele Quarz data book (a<sub>3</sub> = 1.05×10<sup>−4</sup> ppm/K<sup>3</sup>) over assumed camera temperature profiles (a 25 K warm-up, a drifting day) and assumed ±5 arcmin cut-angle errors. That curve moves the relative rate only 15 to 20 ppm over 6 h, so the plain offset hold is already within a 40 ms stand-in tolerance 98–100% of the time at 300 to 1800 s re-syncs; fitting a line matters only at 3600 s (37–43% bad to 9–16%). Theil-Sen and Kalman holds tie with least squares there. They differ only on the assumed 30 ppm wobble: a Kalman filter tuned to fast rate wander (20 ppm per √h) keeps 900 s re-syncs to 0.9% bad where every other fit gives 27% and the offset hold 13%, while at 1800 s every hold fails. Base ppm, temperature profiles, cut-angle errors and wobble are assumed; no real recording.
lede: does a robust fit or a Kalman filter hold a camera clock better between audio re-syncs? On a clock rate computed from a sourced AT-cut crystal curve the plain offset hold is already fine up to 1800 s and every fit ties; only a Kalman filter tuned to an assumed 30 ppm wobble wins. Synthetic audio.
